before.label: Comparative historical sociology
before.description: Compares how states, rights, class relations and collective struggles change. Moore studies agrarian routes; Skocpol combines state breakdown with class and international relations; Tilly follows contention; Mann maps intersecting power networks. Bendix, Goldstone, Somers and Block supply different questions about authority, demography, citizenship and economic institutions. Sewell’s exchange with Skocpol makes ideology an explicit debate.

before.scope_note: A field of competing comparisons, not one state-centered theory. Cases range beyond Europe, but this selection is uneven and does not exhaust regional traditions. Cultural and institutional explanations can be combined; political outcomes are not inevitable stages.

strands.title: Agrarian relations and political routes
strands.focus: Class alliances and rural power produce divergent, often violent paths rather than a smooth democratic sequence.

strands.title: States and revolutionary transformations
strands.focus: State organizations, agrarian classes and international competition enter a combined explanation.

strands.title: Contention and repertoires
strands.focus: Historically specific performances link local claims to wider transformations.
strands.works: Tilly, The Contentious French (1986); political-performances essay (1993–1994)

strands.title: Overlapping networks of power
strands.focus: Forms and reach of power are differentiated rather than enclosed in one homogeneous society.
strands.works: Mann, The Sources of Social Power I (1986)

strands.title: Comparative Marxian transitions
strands.focus: European transitions and divergent state forms frame a contested comparative synthesis.

strands.title: Authority, law and citizenship
strands.focus: Bendix compares authority; Somers examines how local relations and national law shape rights. Their methods are distinct.

strands.title: Reconsidering Polanyi
strands.focus: A specific collaborative engagement with economic institutions broadens the field’s conceptual resources.

strands.title: Population, institutions and state crises
strands.focus: Demographic pressures acquire political effects through institutions and elite relations, not population alone.

strands.title: Ideology within structural explanation
strands.focus: Sewell criticizes a restricted account of ideology; Skocpol acknowledges a problem and responds.

strands.title: Interdependence and group power
strands.focus: Court settings and community exclusion are distinct research scales.
strands.works: The Court Society (1969); The Established and the Outsiders (1965)

strands.title: Sport and regulated excitement
strands.focus: Sport opens a further historical problem of affect and interdependence.

strands.title: Comparing crises and their different outcomes
strands.focus: Goldstone compares England and the Fronde, then distinguishes Castile from the Spanish monarchy’s rebellious peripheries. Similar pressures need not produce identical outcomes. Perry values the comparison but questions how far its claims travel across different societies and periods.

added.relationship: Skocpol questions Sewell’s anonymous conception of culture in revolutionary explanation
added.evidence_note: The reply’s primary opening explicitly proposes a less anonymous approach and questions anthropological cultural systems. This scoped objection coexists with her acknowledgment of an inadequate treatment of ideology; the full rejoinder and French-case reasoning remain unread. It does not represent all historical sociology opposing cultural history.

outcomes.finding: Expanded direct primary check of Skocpol’s reply supports an explicit reciprocal objection, alongside her acknowledgment of Sewell’s criticism. The 1977 Wallerstein review’s opening is now checked, but does not support its later specific critique. Existing comparison preserved; no additional world-system critique inferred.
outcomes.research_limit: Sewell’s full French-case article remains unread. Skocpol’s complete displayed rejoinder opening was read directly, including the concluding reservations paragraph; full 1994 reprint 199–210 remains inaccessible. Original issue metadata confirms 1985 pages 86–96; original article returned 403. Wallerstein-review original PDF redirects to access page; Cambridge reprint provides opening only, not the subsequent critique. Separate official 1994 book excerpt timed out both normally and on escalated curl retry (35 seconds each); no PDF acquired. Searches for original articles and collection copies did not produce an accessible fuller primary text. Secondary discussion and unrelated search hits excluded from argument evidence. These are concrete access limits for the bounded question, not claims to have completed the articles.
